questions.question: The intensity of irrigation for the Kharif season is 50% for an irrigation project with culturable command area of 50,000 hectares. The duty for the Kharif season is 1000 hectare/cumec. Assuming transmission loss of 10%, the required discharge (in cumec, up to two decimal places) at the head of the canal is ______
questions.explanation:
Irrigation Engineering | Canal Discharge Calculation with Transmission Losses

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Culturable Command Area (CCA) = 50,000 hectares
    • Intensity of irrigation (Kharif) = 50%
    • Duty at field (Kharif) = 1000 hectare/cumec
    • Transmission loss = 10% → Efficiency \(\eta = 90\%\)
  • Aim: Calculate required discharge at canal head (in cumec).

3. Core Concepts:

Area to be irrigated: \(A = \text{CCA} \times \text{Intensity}\)

Duty (\(D\)): Area irrigated per unit discharge (hectare/cumec).\[Q_{field} = \dfrac{A}{D}\]

Transmission efficiency:\[\eta = \dfrac{Q_{field}}{Q_{head}} \implies Q_{head} = \dfrac{Q_{field}}{\eta}\]

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Area to be irrigated:\[A = 50{,}000 \times 0.50 = 25{,}000\text{ ha}\]
  2. Discharge at field level:\[Q_{field} = \dfrac{25{,}000}{1000} = 25\text{ cumec}\]
  3. Account for transmission loss:\[\eta = 1 - 0.10 = 0.90\]
  4. Discharge at canal head:\[Q_{head} = \dfrac{25}{0.90} = 27.78\text{ cumec}\]

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 27.78 cumec | Accepted range: 27.00 to 28.00

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q25
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A culvert is designed for a flood frequency of 100 years and a useful life of 20 years. The risk involved in the design of the culvert (in percentage, up to two decimal places) is ______
questions.explanation:
Hydrology & Water Resources | Risk Analysis in Hydraulic Structure Design

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Design flood return period: \(T = 100\text{ years}\)
    • Useful life of structure: \(n = 20\text{ years}\)
  • Aim: Calculate design risk percentage (to two decimal places).

3. Core Concepts:

Annual exceedance probability: \(p = \dfrac{1}{T}\)

Risk (\(R\)): Probability that the design event is exceeded at least once in \(n\) years (Bernoulli trials; flood events are assumed independent year-to-year).\[R = 1 - (1 - p)^n\]

Pitfall: Do not use \(R = n/T\) (linear approximation, invalid for \(n/T > 0.1\)).

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Annual exceedance probability:\[p = \dfrac{1}{100} = 0.01\]
  2. Apply risk formula for \(n = 20\):\[R = 1 - (1 - 0.01)^{20} = 1 - (0.99)^{20}\]
  3. Compute \((0.99)^{20}\):\[(0.99)^{20} = 0.81791\](Using: \(\ln(0.99^{20}) = 20 \times \ln(0.99) = 20 \times (-0.01005) = -0.2010\); \(e^{-0.2010} = 0.8179\))
  4. Calculate risk:\[R = 1 - 0.81791 = 0.18209\]
  5. Convert to percentage:\[R\% = 0.18209 \times 100 = 18.21\%\]

Sanity Check: For \(T = 100\), \(n = 20\), risk ≈ 18–19% (not the 20% linear approximation). ✓

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 18.21% | Accepted range: 17.50 to 18.50

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q26
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question: The matrix \( \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -4 \\ 4 & -2 \end{pmatrix} \) has
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Linear Algebra

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: A \(2 \times 2\) matrix \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -4 \\ 4 & -2 \end{pmatrix}\)
  • Aim: To determine the nature (real or complex) of the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the given matrix.

3. Core Concepts:

Eigenvalues (\(\lambda\)) of a matrix \(A\) are the roots of its characteristic equation: \(\det(A - \lambda I) = 0\).

For a \(2 \times 2\) matrix, the characteristic equation simplifies to: \(\lambda^2 - \text{Tr}(A)\lambda + \det(A) = 0\), where \(\text{Tr}(A)\) is the trace (sum of principal diagonal elements) and \(\det(A)\) is the determinant.

Fundamental Theorem: If a real matrix has complex eigenvalues, the corresponding eigenvectors must also be complex because solving the system \((A - \lambda I)x = 0\) inherently involves complex arithmetic.

4. Solution Method:

  • Compute the trace and determinant of the matrix.
  • Form the characteristic equation and solve for \(\lambda\) to find the eigenvalues.
  • Evaluate whether the roots are real or complex.
  • Infer the nature of the eigenvectors based on the eigenvalues.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Trace of \(A\): \(\text{Tr}(A) = 2 + (-2) = 0\)
  2. Determinant of \(A\): \(\det(A) = (2)(-2) - (-4)(4) = -4 + 16 = 12\)
  3. Characteristic Equation:\[\lambda^2 - 0\cdot\lambda + 12 = 0 \implies \lambda^2 = -12\]
  4. Solve for \(\lambda\):\[\lambda = \pm \sqrt{-12} = \pm i2\sqrt{3}\]Since the discriminant is negative, \(\lambda\) contains an imaginary part \(i\). Thus, the eigenvalues are complex.
  5. Determine Eigenvector Nature: The matrix \(A\) consists purely of real entries. Finding the eigenvector involves finding the null space of \((A - \lambda I)\). Because \(\lambda\) is complex, the resulting matrix \((A - \lambda I)\) will have complex entries, enforcing the resulting null space vectors (eigenvectors) to be complex.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Complex eigenvalues and eigenvectors | Correct option: (D)

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q27
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question: The Laplace transform \( F(s) \) of the exponential function, \( f(t) = e^{at} \) when \( t \ge 0 \), where \( a \) is a constant and \( (s-a) > 0 \), is
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Calculus (Laplace Transforms)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Comprehension
  • Given Data: Function \(f(t) = e^{at}\) for \(t \ge 0\), along with the condition \((s - a) > 0\).
  • Aim: To find the unilateral Laplace transform \(F(s)\) of the exponential function.

3. Core Concepts:

Unilateral Laplace Transform Definition: \(F(s) = L\{f(t)\} = \int_0^\infty f(t) e^{-st} dt\)

Region of Convergence (ROC): The condition \((s - a) > 0\) or \(s > a\) guarantees that the integral converges to a finite value as \(t \to \infty\).

4. Solution Method:

  • Substitute \(f(t) = e^{at}\) directly into the integral definition.
  • Combine the exponential terms.
  • Perform the definite integration from \(0\) to \(\infty\), strictly applying limits to verify the use of the constraint.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Set up the integral:\[F(s) = \int_0^\infty e^{at} \cdot e^{-st}\, dt\]
  2. Combine exponents:\[F(s) = \int_0^\infty e^{-(s-a)t}\, dt\]
  3. Integrate:\[F(s) = \left[\dfrac{e^{-(s-a)t}}{-(s-a)} \right]_0^\infty\]
  4. Apply limits:
    • Upper limit (\(t \to \infty\)): Because \((s-a) > 0\), the exponent \(-(s-a)t\) becomes an increasingly large negative number, so \(e^{-\infty} \to 0\).
    • Lower limit (\(t = 0\)): \(e^{-(s-a) \cdot 0} = e^0 = 1\).
  5. Evaluate:\[F(s) = 0 - \left( \dfrac{1}{-(s-a)} \right) = \dfrac{1}{s-a}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(\dfrac{1}{s-a}\) | Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q28
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question:
The rank of the following matrix is
\( \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 4 & 1 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \)
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Linear Algebra (Matrices)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: A \(3 \times 4\) matrix \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 4 & 1 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\)
  • Aim: To determine the rank of the matrix.

3. Core Concepts:

The Rank of a matrix is the maximum number of linearly independent row or column vectors it contains.

It is determined by converting the matrix into an upper triangular (Row Echelon) form using elementary row operations and counting the number of non-zero rows.

4. Solution Method:

  • Apply Gaussian elimination sequentially to eliminate elements below the main diagonal.
  • Track dependencies to deduce row echelon form.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Initial matrix (rows \(R_1, R_2, R_3\)):\[\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 4 & 1 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\]
  2. Eliminate the first column below \(R_1\):
    • \(R_2 \rightarrow R_2 - 2R_1\): \(\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -2 & 2 & 6 \end{pmatrix}\)
    • \(R_3 \rightarrow R_3 - 4R_1\): \(\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -3 & 3 & 9 \end{pmatrix}\)
    Updated matrix:\[\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 2 & 6 \\ 0 & -3 & 3 & 9 \end{pmatrix}\]
  3. Simplify \(R_2\) and \(R_3\):
    • \(R_2 \rightarrow R_2 / (-2) \implies \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & -1 & -3 \end{pmatrix}\)
    • \(R_3 \rightarrow R_3 / (-3) \implies \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & -1 & -3 \end{pmatrix}\)
  4. Eliminate the second column below \(R_2\):
    • \(R_3 \rightarrow R_3 - R_2 \implies \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\)
    Final Echelon form:\[\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\]
  5. Determine Rank: There are exactly 2 non-zero rows remaining. Therefore, the rank is 2.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 2 | Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q29
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: Two rigid bodies of mass 5 kg and 4 kg are at rest on a frictionless surface until acted upon by a force of 36 N as shown in the figure. The contact force generated between the two bodies is
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mechanics | Dynamics / Kinetics

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Mass of driving block (\(m_1\)) = 5 kg
    • Mass of driven block (\(m_2\)) = 4 kg
    • Applied horizontal push force (\(F\)) = 36 N
    • Surface condition: Frictionless (\(\mu = 0\))
  • Aim: To calculate the internal contact force generated between the two bodies.

3. Core Concepts:

Newton's Second Law of Motion: \(F_{net} = m \cdot a\)

System of Particles: When multiple rigid bodies move together seamlessly, they can be treated as a single composite mass to find systemic acceleration.

Free Body Diagram (FBD): Used to isolate specific bodies and expose internal forces like the normal contact reaction.

4. Solution Method:

  • Consider both blocks as a combined unit to find the shared acceleration \(a\).
  • Isolate the 4 kg block. The only horizontal force causing this block to accelerate is the contact force (\(F_c\)) exerted by the 5 kg block.
  • Apply Newton's Second Law exclusively on the 4 kg block to solve for \(F_c\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate System Acceleration (\(a\)):
    Total mass \(M = m_1 + m_2 = 5\text{ kg} + 4\text{ kg} = 9\text{ kg}\).
    Because there is no friction, the net force is just the applied push force:\[a = \dfrac{F_{net}}{M} = \dfrac{36\text{ N}}{9\text{ kg}} = 4\text{ m/s}^2\]
  2. Isolate the 4 kg block (\(m_2\)):
    Drawing a Free Body Diagram for the 4 kg block alone, we see there are no resisting frictional forces. The only horizontal force acting on it is the forward contact force (\(F_c\)) from the 5 kg block.
  3. Apply Newton's Second Law to the 4 kg block:\[F_c = m_2 \cdot a = 4\text{ kg} \times 4\text{ m/s}^2 = 16.0\text{ N}\]

Alternative Check: Isolate the 5 kg block. \(F_{net} = 36 - F_c = m_1 \cdot a \implies 36 - F_c = 5 \times 4 \implies F_c = 16\text{ N}\). The result is consistent.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 16.0 N | Correct option: (D)

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q30
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Steel Tension, Compression Members & Plastic Analysis
questions.question:
Four bolts P, Q, R and S of equal diameter are used for a bracket subjected to a load of 130 kN as shown in the figure.



The force in bolt P is
questions.explanation:
Structural Engineering | Steel Structures (Bolted Connections)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Four bolts arranged in a rectangle: P, Q, R, S
    • Eccentric load (\(P\)) = 130 kN acting vertically downwards
    • Horizontal gauge distance between bolts = 100 mm
    • Vertical pitch distance between bolts = 240 mm
    • Eccentricity (\(e\)) of the load from the centre-line of the bolt group = 200 mm
  • Aim: To find the resultant force on the most stressed bolt (Bolt P).

3. Core Concepts:

Eccentric Bolted Connection (In-plane bending): An eccentric load \(P\) can be resolved into a direct downward shear force acting at the centre of gravity (CG) of the bolt group, and a twisting moment \(M = P \times e\).

Direct Shear Force (\(F_d\)): Distributed equally among all identical bolts: \(F_d = \dfrac{P}{n}\), acting parallel to the applied load.

Torsional Shear Force (\(F_t\)): Proportional to the radial distance (\(r\)) of the bolt from the CG: \(F_t = \dfrac{M \cdot r}{\sum r^2}\). Its direction is perpendicular to the radial vector.

Resultant Force (\(F_R\)): Vector sum of \(F_d\) and \(F_t\) using Cartesian components.

4. Solution Method:

  • Identify the coordinates of Bolt P relative to the CG to find its radial distance \(r\).
  • Compute the direct shear force component \(F_{dy}\).
  • Compute the torsional moment \(M\).
  • Determine the \(x\) and \(y\) components of the torsional shear force (\(F_{tx}\) and \(F_{ty}\)) for Bolt P.
  • Calculate the resultant force \(F_R\) using the combined orthogonal components.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Geometry of the Bolt Group:
    Taking the CG of the 4 bolts as the origin \((0,0)\):
    • Horizontal distance from CG to bolt: \(x = \dfrac{100}{2} = 50\text{ mm}\)
    • Vertical distance from CG to bolt: \(y = \dfrac{240}{2} = 120\text{ mm}\)
    • Radial distance squared for one bolt: \(r^2 = x^2 + y^2 = 50^2 + 120^2 = 2500 + 14400 = 16900\text{ mm}^2\)
    • For 4 bolts: \(\sum r^2 = 4 \times 16900 = 67600\text{ mm}^2\)
  2. Direct Shear Force (\(F_d\)):\[F_{d} = \dfrac{P}{n} = \dfrac{130\text{ kN}}{4} = 32.5\text{ kN}\](Acts vertically downwards, so \(F_{dy} = 32.5\text{ kN}\))
  3. Torsional Shear Force on Bolt P:
    • Moment: \(M = P \times e = 130\text{ kN} \times 200\text{ mm} = 26000\text{ kN·mm}\) (Clockwise)
    • Bolt P is in the top-right quadrant at \((50, 120)\). Since \(M\) is clockwise, the torsional force vector at P points rightward and downward.
    • Horizontal component: \(F_{tx} = \dfrac{M \cdot y}{\sum r^2} = \dfrac{26000 \times 120}{67600} = 46.154\text{ kN}\) (Rightwards)
    • Vertical component: \(F_{ty} = \dfrac{M \cdot x}{\sum r^2} = \dfrac{26000 \times 50}{67600} = 19.231\text{ kN}\) (Downwards)
  4. Resultant Force on Bolt P (\(F_R\)):
    • Total horizontal force: \(\Sigma F_x = F_{tx} = 46.154\text{ kN}\)
    • Total vertical force: \(\Sigma F_y = F_{dy} + F_{ty} = 32.5 + 19.231 = 51.731\text{ kN}\)
    \[F_R = \sqrt{(\Sigma F_x)^2 + (\Sigma F_y)^2} = \sqrt{(46.154)^2 + (51.731)^2}\]\[F_R = \sqrt{2130.19 + 2676.10} = \sqrt{4806.29} \approx 69.32\text{ kN}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 69.32 kN | Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q31
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Limit State Design of Beams & Slabs
questions.question: A singly-reinforced rectangular concrete beam of width 300 mm and effective depth 400 mm is to be designed using M25 grade concrete and Fe500 grade reinforcing steel. For the beam to be under-reinforced, the maximum number of 16 mm diameter reinforcing bars that can be provided is
questions.explanation:
Civil Engineering | Reinforced Concrete Design (Limit State Method)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Width of beam (\(b\)) = 300 mm
    • Effective depth (\(d\)) = 400 mm
    • Concrete Grade = M25 (\(f_{ck} = 25\text{ MPa}\))
    • Steel Grade = Fe500 (\(f_y = 500\text{ MPa}\))
    • Bar diameter (\(\phi\)) = 16 mm
  • Aim: To determine the maximum integer number of 16 mm bars that keeps the beam strictly under-reinforced (\(A_{st} \le A_{st,lim}\)).

3. Core Concepts (IS 456:2000):

Limiting Neutral Axis Depth (\(x_{u,max}\)): For Fe500, \(x_{u,max} = 0.46d\) (IS 456:2000, Clause 38.1).

Balanced Section: The maximum area of tension steel (\(A_{st,lim}\)) allowed before a section becomes over-reinforced is found by equating total compression to total tension at the limiting neutral axis depth.

  • Compressive force: \(C = 0.36\, f_{ck}\, b\, x_{u,max}\)
  • Tensile force: \(T = 0.87\, f_y\, A_{st,lim}\)

Under-Reinforced Condition: Requires provided steel area \(A_{st} \le A_{st,lim}\).

4. Solution Method:

  • Calculate \(x_{u,max}\).
  • Equate \(C = T\) to compute the limiting area of steel \(A_{st,lim}\).
  • Calculate the cross-sectional area of a single 16 mm bar (\(a_{st}\)).
  • Divide \(A_{st,lim}\) by \(a_{st}\) to find the limiting number of bars.
  • Round down to the nearest whole integer to ensure the section stays under-reinforced.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Limiting Neutral Axis (\(x_{u,max}\)):\[x_{u,max} = 0.46 \times 400\text{ mm} = 184\text{ mm}\]
  2. Limiting Area of Steel (\(A_{st,lim}\)):
    Equating forces \(C = T\):\[0.36\, f_{ck}\, b\, x_{u,max} = 0.87\, f_y\, A_{st,lim}\]\[0.36 \times 25 \times 300 \times 184 = 0.87 \times 500 \times A_{st,lim}\]\[496800\text{ N} = 435 \cdot A_{st,lim}\]\[A_{st,lim} = \dfrac{496800}{435} = 1142.07\text{ mm}^2\]
  3. Area of one 16 mm bar (\(a_{st}\)):\[a_{st} = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \times (16)^2 \approx 201.06\text{ mm}^2\]
  4. Maximum Number of Bars (\(n\)):\[n = \dfrac{A_{st,lim}}{a_{st}} = \dfrac{1142.07}{201.06} = 5.68\text{ bars}\]Since an integer number of bars is required, and providing 6 bars (\(6 \times 201.06 = 1206.36\text{ mm}^2\)) would exceed the limit and make the section over-reinforced, we must round down.\[n_{max} = 5\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 5 | Correct option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q32
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: A 3 m high vertical earth retaining wall retains a dry granular backfill with angle of internal friction of 30° and unit weight of 20 kN/m³. If the wall is prevented from yielding (no movement), the total horizontal thrust (in kN per unit length) on the wall is
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Lateral Earth Pressure

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension / Application
  • Given Data:
    • Height of retaining wall (\(H\)) = 3 m
    • Unit weight of backfill (\(\gamma\)) = 20 kN/m³
    • Angle of internal friction (\(\phi\)) = 30°
    • Wall condition: "Prevented from yielding" (No movement)
  • Aim: To calculate the total horizontal thrust per unit length of the wall.

3. Core Concepts:

Earth Pressure Condition: When a retaining wall is strictly prevented from yielding or moving, the soil is in a state of Earth Pressure at Rest.

Coefficient of Earth Pressure at Rest (\(K_0\)): Estimated using Jaky's empirical formula for normally consolidated granular soils: \(K_0 = 1 - \sin\phi\).

Lateral Earth Pressure Distribution: Varies triangularly with depth \(z\), such that horizontal stress \(\sigma_h = K_0 \cdot \gamma \cdot z\).

Total Horizontal Thrust (\(P_0\)): The area of the triangular pressure distribution diagram:\[P_0 = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot K_0 \cdot \gamma \cdot H^2\]

4. Solution Method:

  • Calculate the at-rest coefficient \(K_0\) using the given friction angle.
  • Substitute \(K_0\), \(\gamma\), and \(H\) into the formula for total thrust.
  • Solve to find \(P_0\) in kN/m.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate \(K_0\):\[K_0 = 1 - \sin(30^\circ) = 1 - 0.5 = 0.5\]
  2. Calculate horizontal stress at the base of the wall (\(z = H\)):\[(\sigma_h)_{base} = K_0 \cdot \gamma \cdot H = 0.5 \times 20\text{ kN/m}^3 \times 3\text{ m} = 30\text{ kN/m}^2\]
  3. Calculate Total Thrust (\(P_0\)):
    The thrust is the area of the triangular stress block.\[P_0 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times (\text{Base Stress}) \times \text{Height}\]\[P_0 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 30\text{ kN/m}^2 \times 3\text{ m} = 45\text{ kN/m}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 45 kN/m | Correct option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q33
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question:
Three soil specimens (Soil 1, Soil 2 and Soil 3), each 150 mm long and 100 mm diameter, are placed in series in a constant head flow set-up as shown in the figure. Suitable screens are provided at the boundaries of the specimens to keep them intact. The values of coefficient of permeability of Soil 1, Soil 2 and Soil 3 are 0.01, 0.003 and 0.03 cm/s, respectively.



The value of h in the set-up is
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Permeability and Seepage

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Lengths of soil specimens: \(L_1 = L_2 = L_3 = 150\text{ mm}\)
    • Diameter of soil specimens: \(D = 100\text{ mm}\) (Cross-sectional area \(A\) is constant)
    • Permeability of Soil 1: \(k_1 = 0.01\text{ cm/s}\)
    • Permeability of Soil 2: \(k_2 = 0.003\text{ cm/s}\)
    • Permeability of Soil 3: \(k_3 = 0.03\text{ cm/s}\)
    • Total head difference between upstream (left) and downstream (right) reservoirs: \(\Delta H = 560\text{ mm}\)
  • Aim: Find the value of \(h\), which the diagram shows as the piezometric head difference between the standpipe at the entry of Soil 3 and the water level of the right reservoir. Thus, \(h\) equals the head loss across Soil 3 alone (\(\Delta h_3\)).

3. Core Concepts:

Darcy's Law: \(Q = k \cdot i \cdot A\)

Continuity Equation for Series Flow: For soils connected in series with a constant cross-sectional area, the discharge \(Q\) and the discharge velocity \(v\) are constant across all layers.\[v = k_1 i_1 = k_2 i_2 = k_3 i_3\]

Hydraulic Gradient: \(i = \dfrac{\Delta h}{L}\)

Total Head Loss: \(\Delta H = \Delta h_1 + \Delta h_2 + \Delta h_3\)

4. Solution Method:

Since velocity \(v\) and length \(L\) are constant for all three soils, the head loss in each soil layer is inversely proportional to its permeability. Express the head loss of Soil 1 and Soil 2 in terms of the head loss of Soil 3 (\(\Delta h_3\)). Sum them up and equate to the total head loss (\(\Delta H = 560\text{ mm}\)) to solve for \(\Delta h_3\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Establish relationship between head losses:\[k_1 \dfrac{\Delta h_1}{L_1} = k_2 \dfrac{\Delta h_2}{L_2} = k_3 \dfrac{\Delta h_3}{L_3}\]Since \(L_1 = L_2 = L_3\):\[k_1 \Delta h_1 = k_2 \Delta h_2 = k_3 \Delta h_3\]
  2. Express \(\Delta h_1\) and \(\Delta h_2\) in terms of \(\Delta h_3\):\[\Delta h_1 = \dfrac{k_3}{k_1} \Delta h_3 = \dfrac{0.03}{0.01} \Delta h_3 = 3\,\Delta h_3\]\[\Delta h_2 = \dfrac{k_3}{k_2} \Delta h_3 = \dfrac{0.03}{0.003} \Delta h_3 = 10\,\Delta h_3\]
  3. Apply total head loss constraint:\[\Delta H = \Delta h_1 + \Delta h_2 + \Delta h_3 = 560\text{ mm}\]\[3\,\Delta h_3 + 10\,\Delta h_3 + 1\,\Delta h_3 = 560\text{ mm}\]\[14\,\Delta h_3 = 560\text{ mm}\]
  4. Solve for \(\Delta h_3\):\[\Delta h_3 = \dfrac{560}{14} = 40\text{ mm}\]Since \(h\) in the figure is the head loss across Soil 3, \(h = 40\text{ mm}\).

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 40 mm | Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q34
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: In a 5 m wide rectangular channel, the velocity u distribution in the vertical direction y is given by \( u = 1.25y^{\frac{1}{6}} \). The distance y is measured from the channel bed. If the flow depth is 2 m, the discharge per unit width of the channel is
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Open Channel Flow

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Channel width: \(B = 5\text{ m}\)
    • Velocity distribution: \(u(y) = 1.25\, y^{1/6}\text{ m/s}\) (where \(y\) is distance from the bed)
    • Flow depth: \(h = 2\text{ m}\)
  • Aim: Calculate the discharge per unit width (\(q\)) in \(\text{m}^3\text{/s/m}\).

3. Core Concepts:

Discharge per Unit Width (\(q\)): Represents the integration of the velocity profile over the entire depth of flow.\[q = \int_{0}^{h} u(y)\, dy\]

4. Solution Method:

Direct integration of the given power-law velocity distribution formula with respect to \(y\), evaluated from the bed (\(y = 0\)) to the free surface (\(y = 2\text{ m}\)).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Set up the integral:\[q = \int_{0}^{2} 1.25\, y^{1/6}\, dy\]
  2. Integrate:\[q = 1.25 \left[\dfrac{y^{\dfrac{1}{6}+1}}{\dfrac{1}{6}+1} \right]_{0}^{2} = 1.25 \left[\dfrac{y^{7/6}}{7/6} \right]_{0}^{2}\]\[q = 1.25 \times \dfrac{6}{7} \left[y^{7/6} \right]_{0}^{2} = \dfrac{7.5}{7} \left( 2^{7/6} - 0 \right)\]
  3. Calculate the final value:\[2^{7/6} = 2^1 \times 2^{1/6} \approx 2 \times 1.12246 = 2.2449\]\[q = \left(\dfrac{7.5}{7}\right) \times 2.2449 \approx 1.0714 \times 2.2449 = 2.405\text{ m}^3\text{/s/m}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 2.40 \(\text{m}^3\text{/s/m}\) | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q35
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: A car follows a slow moving truck (travelling at a speed of 10 m/s) on a two-lane two-way highway. The car reduces its speed to 10 m/s and follows the truck maintaining a distance of 16 m from the truck. On finding a clear gap in the opposing traffic stream, the car accelerates at an average rate of 4 m/s², overtakes the truck and returns to its original lane. When it returns to its original lane, the distance between the car and the truck is 16 m. The total distance covered by the car during this period (from the time it leaves its lane and subsequently returns to its lane after overtaking) is
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Highway Geometric Design

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Speed of truck: \(v_t = 10\text{ m/s}\) (Constant)
    • Initial speed of car: \(v_c = 10\text{ m/s}\)
    • Acceleration of car during overtaking: \(a = 4\text{ m/s}^2\)
    • Initial gap maintained before overtaking: \(s_1 = 16\text{ m}\)
    • Final gap maintained after returning to lane: \(s_2 = 16\text{ m}\)
  • Aim: Calculate the total distance covered by the car from leaving its lane to returning after overtaking.

3. Core Concepts:

Relative Kinematics: To safely overtake, the car must cover the relative distance of both initial and final gaps with respect to the moving truck.
(Note: Per standard IRC Overtaking Sight Distance analysis, since specific vehicle lengths aren't provided, the relative distance to clear is simply the sum of the gaps.)

Equations of Motion:\[S_{rel} = u_{rel}\,t + \dfrac{1}{2}a_{rel}\,t^2\]\[S_{car} = v_c\,t + \dfrac{1}{2}a_{car}\,t^2\]

4. Solution Method:

Calculate the overtaking maneuver time (\(t\)) by analyzing the relative motion between the car and the truck. Once \(t\) is obtained, compute the absolute distance covered by the car using its own acceleration and initial velocity.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Define Relative Variables:
    • Relative initial velocity: \(u_{rel} = 10 - 10 = 0\text{ m/s}\)
    • Relative acceleration: \(a_{rel} = 4 - 0 = 4\text{ m/s}^2\)
    • Total relative distance to be covered: \(S_{rel} = s_1 + s_2 = 16 + 16 = 32\text{ m}\)
  2. Calculate Time to Overtake (\(t\)):\[S_{rel} = u_{rel}\,t + \dfrac{1}{2}a_{rel}\,t^2\]\[32 = 0 \cdot t + \dfrac{1}{2}(4)t^2\]\[32 = 2t^2 \implies t^2 = 16 \implies t = 4\text{ seconds}\]
  3. Calculate Total Absolute Distance Covered by the Car (\(S_{car}\)):\[S_{car} = v_c\,t + \dfrac{1}{2}a\,t^2\]\[S_{car} = (10 \times 4) + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times (4)^2\]\[S_{car} = 40 + 2(16) = 40 + 32 = 72\text{ m}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 72 m | Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q36
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question: A level instrument at a height of 1.320 m has been placed at a station having a Reduced Level (RL) of 112.565 m. The instrument reads -2.835 m on a levelling staff held at the bottom of a bridge deck. The RL (in m) of the bottom of the bridge deck is
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Levelling

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Reduced Level (RL) of station: \(112.565\text{ m}\)
    • Height of instrument setup: \(1.320\text{ m}\)
    • Levelling staff reading (inverted, at bottom of bridge deck): \(-2.835\text{ m}\)
  • Aim: Calculate the RL of the bottom of the bridge deck.

3. Core Concepts:

Height of Instrument (HI) Method:\[HI = RL_{\text{station}} + \text{Setup Height}\]

Inverted Staff Convention: When a point is above the line of sight (e.g., a ceiling or soffit of a deck), the staff is held inverted. The reading is treated as negative algebraically.\[RL_{\text{point}} = HI - \text{Staff Reading}\]

4. Solution Method:

First, calculate the elevation of the line of sight (HI). Then, subtract the negative staff reading to obtain the elevation of the bridge deck. Subtracting a negative inherently adds it, reflecting that the point physically sits above the line of sight.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Height of Instrument (HI):\[HI = 112.565\text{ m} + 1.320\text{ m} = 113.885\text{ m}\]
  2. Calculate RL of Bridge Deck:\[RL_{\text{deck}} = HI - (\text{Staff Reading})\]\[RL_{\text{deck}} = 113.885 - (-2.835)\]\[RL_{\text{deck}} = 113.885 + 2.835 = 116.720\text{ m}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 116.720 m | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q37
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question: The value (up to two decimal places) of a line integral \(\displaystyle \int_C \vec{F}(\vec{r}) \cdot d\vec{r} \), for \( \vec{F}(\vec{r}) = x^2\hat{i} + y^2\hat{j} \) along C which is a straight line joining (0,0) to (1,1) is ______
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Vector Calculus

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Vector Field: \(\vec{F}(\vec{r}) = x^2\,\hat{i} + y^2\,\hat{j}\)
    • Path of integration \(C\): Straight line joining points \((0,0)\) to \((1,1)\)
  • Aim: Evaluate the line integral \(\displaystyle\int_C \vec{F}(\vec{r}) \cdot d\vec{r}\) up to two decimal places.

3. Core Concepts:

Work Done / Line Integral:\[\int_C \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = \int_C (F_x\,dx + F_y\,dy)\]

Parametrization of a Line: For a straight line joining the origin to point \((1,1)\), the equation of the path is \(y = x\). Therefore, \(dy = dx\).

Sanity Check: The vector field is conservative because \(\nabla \times \vec{F} = 0\). The integral is path-independent, making direct evaluation along \(y = x\) fully valid.

4. Solution Method:

Substitute the equation of the line (\(y = x\) and \(dy = dx\)) into the line integral formula to convert it into a single-variable definite integral, then solve.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Set up the differential path vector:\[d\vec{r} = dx\,\hat{i} + dy\,\hat{j}\]
  2. Form the dot product:\[\vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = (x^2\,\hat{i} + y^2\,\hat{j}) \cdot (dx\,\hat{i} + dy\,\hat{j}) = x^2\,dx + y^2\,dy\]
  3. Apply path parametrization (\(y = x\), \(dy = dx\)):\[\int_C \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = \int_{x=0}^{x=1} (x^2\,dx + x^2\,dx) = \int_{0}^{1} 2x^2\,dx\]
  4. Integrate and evaluate bounds:\[= \left[\dfrac{2x^3}{3} \right]_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{2(1)^3}{3} - 0 = \dfrac{2}{3} \approx 0.67\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.67 | Accepted key range: 0.60 to 0.70

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q38
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: An 8 m long simply-supported elastic beam of rectangular cross-section (100 mm × 200 mm) is subjected to a uniformly distributed load of 10 kN/m over its entire span. The maximum principal stress (in MPa, up to two decimal places) at a point located at the extreme compression edge of a cross-section and at 2 m from the support is ______
questions.explanation:
Solid Mechanics | Principal Stresses

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application & Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Beam type: Simply-supported elastic beam
    • Span: \(L = 8\text{ m}\)
    • Rectangular cross-section: Width \(b = 100\text{ mm}\), Depth \(d = 200\text{ mm}\)
    • Load: UDL \(w = 10\text{ kN/m}\) over the entire span
    • Target Location: \(x = 2\text{ m}\) from the support, at the extreme compression edge (top fiber)
  • Aim: Find the maximum principal stress (in MPa) at the specified point.

3. Core Concepts:

Bending Moment: For a simply supported beam with a UDL, the moment at distance \(x\) is:\[M(x) = \dfrac{wLx}{2} - \dfrac{wx^2}{2}\]

Flexural Formula: \(\sigma_x = -\dfrac{M \cdot y}{I}\), where the negative sign implies compression.

Moment of Inertia: \(I = \dfrac{bd^3}{12}\) for a rectangular section.

Principal Stresses (2D plane stress):\[\sigma_{1,2} = \dfrac{\sigma_x + \sigma_y}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\sigma_x - \sigma_y}{2}\right)^2 + \tau_{xy}^2}\]

Boundary Condition for Shear: At the extreme top and bottom fibers of a cross-section, \(\tau_{xy} = 0\). Hence, normal stresses directly correspond to principal stresses.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate the bending moment at \(x = 2\text{ m}\).
  2. Determine the section's moment of inertia (\(I\)).
  3. Calculate the normal bending stress (\(\sigma_x\)) at the top extreme compression edge (\(y = d/2\)).
  4. Because \(\tau_{xy} = 0\), the principal stresses are \(\sigma_x\) and \(0\).
  5. Common Pitfall: "Maximum principal stress" refers to the algebraically largest principal stress (\(\sigma_1\)), not the maximum magnitude. Always check signs.

Sanity Note: The resulting bending stress is around 90 MPa, which exceeds typical concrete strengths, but as the problem specifies an "elastic beam," we proceed purely based on theoretical linear elastic solid mechanics.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate the Bending Moment at \(x = 2\text{ m}\):
    Support reactions: \(R_A = R_B = \dfrac{wL}{2} = \dfrac{10 \times 8}{2} = 40\text{ kN}\)\[M(x=2) = (R_A \times 2) - \left(w \times 2 \times \dfrac{2}{2}\right) = (40 \times 2) - (10 \times 2) = 80 - 20 = 60\text{ kNm}\]Convert: \(M = 60 \times 10^6\text{ N·mm}\)
  2. Calculate Moment of Inertia (\(I\)):\[I = \dfrac{b \cdot d^3}{12} = \dfrac{100 \times 200^3}{12} = 66.67 \times 10^6\text{ mm}^4\]
  3. Calculate Flexural Stress at Compression Edge:
    Distance to extreme top fiber: \(y = \dfrac{200}{2} = 100\text{ mm}\)\[\sigma_x = -\dfrac{M \cdot y}{I} = -\dfrac{60 \times 10^6 \times 100}{66.67 \times 10^6} = -90\text{ MPa}\]
  4. Identify Principal Stresses:
    State of stress at top fiber: \(\sigma_x = -90\text{ MPa}\), \(\sigma_y = 0\), \(\tau_{xy} = 0\)
    \(\sigma_1 = 0\text{ MPa}\), \(\sigma_2 = -90\text{ MPa}\)
  5. Determine Maximum Principal Stress:
    Algebraically, \(0 > -90\). Therefore, the maximum principal stress is \(\mathbf{0}\) MPa.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.00 MPa | Accepted key range: 0.0 to 0.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q39
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
A prismatic beam P-Q-R of flexural rigidity \( EI = 1 \times 10^4 \text{ kNm}^2 \) is subjected to a moment of 180 kNm at Q as shown in the figure.



The rotation at Q (in rad, up to two decimal places) is ______
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Deflection of Beams

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Continuous prismatic beam P-Q-R; P and R are fixed supports, Q is an internal roller support
    • Spans: \(L_{PQ} = 5\text{ m}\), \(L_{QR} = 4\text{ m}\)
    • Flexural rigidity: \(EI = 1 \times 10^4\text{ kNm}^2\)
    • Loading: External concentrated moment of \(180\text{ kNm}\) applied at joint Q
  • Aim: Find the rotation at joint Q (in radians).

3. Core Concepts:

Rotational Stiffness (\(k\)): For a member with far-end fixed, the rotational stiffness is \(k = \dfrac{4EI}{L}\).

Equilibrium Condition:\[M_{applied} = \left(\sum k\right) \cdot \theta_Q\]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Identify boundary conditions (supports P and R are fixed, preventing rotation).
  2. Compute the flexural stiffness of spans QP and QR at joint Q.
  3. Apply joint equilibrium to find the common rotation \(\theta_Q\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Rotational Stiffness of spans QP and QR:
    For span QP (far end P is fixed):\[k_{QP} = \dfrac{4EI}{L_{PQ}} = \dfrac{4EI}{5} = 0.8\,EI\]For span QR (far end R is fixed):\[k_{QR} = \dfrac{4EI}{L_{QR}} = \dfrac{4EI}{4} = 1.0\,EI\]
  2. Total Joint Stiffness:\[\sum k_Q = k_{QP} + k_{QR} = 0.8\,EI + 1.0\,EI = 1.8\,EI\]
  3. Joint Equilibrium Equation:
    The externally applied moment is balanced by the joint's internal stiffness rotation:\[M = (\sum k_Q) \cdot \theta_Q\]\[180 = 1.8\,EI \cdot \theta_Q\]\[\theta_Q = \dfrac{180}{1.8\,EI} = \dfrac{100}{EI}\]
  4. Calculate Final Rotation:
    Substitute \(EI = 10^4\text{ kNm}^2\):\[\theta_Q = \dfrac{100}{10^4} = 0.01\text{ rad}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.01 rad | Accepted key range: 0.01 to 0.01 (or −0.01 to −0.01)

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q40
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: A prismatic propped cantilever beam of span \( L \) and plastic moment capacity \( M_p \) is subjected to a concentrated load at its mid-span. If the collapse load of the beam is \( \alpha \dfrac{M_p}{L} \), the value of \( \alpha \) is ______
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Plastic Analysis

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Beam type: Prismatic propped cantilever (one end fixed, one end simply supported)
    • Span = \(L\)
    • Plastic moment capacity = \(M_p\)
    • Load: Concentrated load at mid-span
    • Collapse load relation: \(P_u = \alpha\,\dfrac{M_p}{L}\)
  • Aim: Determine the value of coefficient \(\alpha\).

3. Core Concepts:

Kinematic Method of Plasticity: Equating the internal work done by plastic hinges to the external work done by applied loads during a virtual collapse mechanism.

Hinge Formation: In a propped cantilever under a point load, plastic hinges form at the fixed support (maximum negative moment) and exactly under the point load (maximum positive moment). The simply supported end cannot form a plastic hinge as its moment is zero.

Work Equations:
Internal Work: \(W_I = \sum M_p \cdot \theta_{hinge}\)
External Work: \(W_E = P_u \cdot \delta_{load}\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Sketch a virtual collapse mechanism showing hinge locations.
  2. Formulate geometric relations between the mid-span deflection (\(\delta\)) and hinge rotations (\(\theta\)).
  3. Set up the Internal Work and External Work equations.
  4. Equate \(W_I = W_E\) to solve for \(P_u\) and extract \(\alpha\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Deflection Geometry:
    Let fixed end = A, load at mid-span = C, simple support = B.
    Let virtual downward deflection at C = \(\delta\).
    • Rotation of span AC (hinge rotation at A): \(\theta_A = \dfrac{\delta}{L/2} = \dfrac{2\delta}{L}\)
    • Rotation of span CB: \(\theta_B = \dfrac{\delta}{L/2} = \dfrac{2\delta}{L}\)
    • Relative plastic hinge rotation at C: \(\theta_C = \theta_A + \theta_B = \dfrac{2\delta}{L} + \dfrac{2\delta}{L} = \dfrac{4\delta}{L}\)
  2. External Work (\(W_E\)):\[W_E = P_u \cdot \delta\]
  3. Internal Work (\(W_I\)): (No plastic hinge at simple support B)\[W_I = M_p \cdot \theta_A + M_p \cdot \theta_C = M_p\left(\dfrac{2\delta}{L}\right) + M_p\left(\dfrac{4\delta}{L}\right) = \dfrac{6M_p \cdot \delta}{L}\]
  4. Equating Works:\[P_u \cdot \delta = \dfrac{6M_p \cdot \delta}{L} \implies P_u = \dfrac{6M_p}{L}\]
  5. Compare to Given Formula:
    Given \(P_u = \alpha\,\dfrac{M_p}{L}\), therefore \(\alpha = 6\).

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 6.0 | Accepted key range: 6.0 to 6.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q41
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Limit State Design of Beams & Slabs
questions.question:
A 6 m long simply-supported beam is prestressed as shown in the figure.



The beam carries a uniformly distributed load of 6 kN/m over its entire span. If the effective flexural rigidity \( EI = 2 \times 10^4 \text{ kNm}^2 \) and the effective prestressing force is 200 kN, the net increase in length of the prestressing cable (in mm, up to two decimal places) is ______
questions.explanation:
Pre-stressed Concrete | Deflection & Strain

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Simply-supported span: \(L = 6\text{ m}\)
    • Effective flexural rigidity: \(EI = 2 \times 10^4\text{ kNm}^2\)
    • Effective prestressing force: \(P = 200\text{ kN}\)
    • Constant eccentricity: \(e = 50\text{ mm} = 0.05\text{ m}\) (below the neutral axis)
    • Applied UDL: \(w = 6\text{ kN/m}\) over entire span
  • Aim: Calculate the net increase in length of the prestressing cable (in mm) strictly due to flexural curvature.

3. Core Concepts:

Flexural Strain: The longitudinal strain at depth \(y\) from the neutral axis due to pure bending is:\[\varepsilon_x = \dfrac{y}{\rho} = \dfrac{M_{net} \cdot y}{EI}\]

Cable Elongation: The change in length of a fiber (cable) at eccentricity \(e\) from the neutral axis is the integral of bending strain across the span:\[\Delta L = \int_{0}^{L} \varepsilon_x\, dx = \int_{0}^{L} \dfrac{M_{net} \cdot e}{EI}\, dx = \dfrac{e}{EI} \int_{0}^{L} M_{net}\, dx\]

Note: Since the cross-sectional area \(A\) is not provided, the primary uniform axial compressive shortening (\(-PL/AE\)) is considered negligible compared to bending deformation.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Identify moments: Applied downward UDL causes positive (sagging) bending; prestress force causes negative (hogging) bending.
  2. The integral \(\displaystyle \int M_{net}\,dx\) is equivalent to calculating the net Area of the Bending Moment Diagrams (BMD).
  3. Compute area of UDL BMD and area of Prestress BMD.
  4. Use the derived flexural strain formula to find the elongation.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Area of Moment Diagram due to UDL (\(A_1\)):
    The BMD for UDL is a parabola with maximum ordinate \(M_{max} = \dfrac{wL^2}{8}\).\[A_1 = \dfrac{2}{3} \cdot L \cdot M_{max} = \dfrac{2}{3} \cdot L \cdot \dfrac{wL^2}{8} = \dfrac{wL^3}{12}\]\[A_1 = \dfrac{6 \times 6^3}{12} = \dfrac{6 \times 216}{12} = 108\text{ kNm}^2\quad\text{(tension at cable level)}\]
  2. Area of Moment Diagram due to Prestress (\(A_2\)):
    The BMD for a straight eccentric cable is a rectangle with constant ordinate \(M_p = P \cdot e\).\[A_2 = P \cdot e \cdot L = 200 \times 0.05 \times 6 = 60\text{ kNm}^2\quad\text{(compression at cable level)}\]
  3. Net Bending Moment Area (\(A_{net}\)):\[A_{net} = A_1 - A_2 = 108 - 60 = 48\text{ kNm}^2\]
  4. Net Increase in Cable Length (\(\Delta L\)):\[\Delta L = \dfrac{A_{net} \cdot e}{EI} = \dfrac{48 \times 0.05}{2 \times 10^4} = \dfrac{2.4}{20000} = 0.00012\text{ m}\]Convert to mm: \(0.00012 \times 1000 = 0.12\text{ mm}\)

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.12 mm | Accepted key range: 0.10 to 0.12

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q42
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
A cable PQ of length 25 m is supported at two ends at the same level as shown in the figure. The horizontal distance between the supports is 20 m. A point load of 150 kN is applied at point R which divides it into two equal parts.



Neglecting the self-weight of the cable, the tension (in kN, in integer value) in the cable due to the applied load will be ______
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Cables

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Flexible cable total length = \(25\text{ m}\)
    • Supported at equal level P and Q
    • Horizontal span between P and Q = \(20\text{ m}\)
    • Single point load \(W = 150\text{ kN}\) applied at R
    • R divides horizontal span into equal halves (\(10\text{ m}\) each)
  • Aim: Find the tension \(T\) (in kN) in the cable due to the applied load.

3. Core Concepts:

Static Equilibrium of Cables: A highly flexible cable carrying a single point load transforms into two straight line segments creating a V-shape.

Symmetry Geometry: Because the load is centrally applied and supports are at equal level, the tension \(T\) is identical on both sides, creating symmetric 2D right-angled triangles.

Joint Vertical Equilibrium:\[\sum F_y = 0 \implies 2 \cdot T \cdot \sin(\theta) = W_{applied}\]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Use geometric symmetry to find the length of individual cable segment PR and its horizontal projection.
  2. Apply the Pythagorean theorem to calculate the central sag/dip (\(h\)) at point R.
  3. Find \(\sin(\theta)\) where \(\theta\) is the angle the cable makes with the horizontal.
  4. Establish vertical equilibrium at node R to calculate \(T\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Cable Geometry Configuration:
    Due to strict symmetry:
    • Horizontal distance from support P to mid-point R: \(\dfrac{20}{2} = 10\text{ m}\)
    • Length of sloped cable segment PR: \(\dfrac{25}{2} = 12.5\text{ m}\)
  2. Finding the Central Dip (\(h\)):
    Applying Pythagoras to the triangle formed by support P and point R:\[10^2 + h^2 = 12.5^2\]\[100 + h^2 = 156.25\]\[h^2 = 56.25 \implies h = 7.5\text{ m}\]Sanity Check: Ratios \(10 : 7.5 : 12.5\) match a scaled classic \(4:3:5\) right triangle.
  3. Resolving Forces at Node R:\[\sin(\theta) = \dfrac{h}{\text{Length}_{PR}} = \dfrac{7.5}{12.5} = 0.6\]Applying vertical equilibrium (\(\sum F_y = 0\)):\[2 \cdot T \cdot \sin(\theta) = 150\]\[2 \cdot T \cdot 0.6 = 150\]\[1.2\,T = 150\]\[T = \dfrac{150}{1.2} = 125\text{ kN}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 125 kN | Accepted key range: 125 to 125

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q43
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: The compression curve (void ratio, e vs. effective stress, σ'v) for a certain clayey soil is a straight line in a semi-logarithmic plot and it passes through the points (e = 1.2; σ'v = 50 kPa) and (e = 0.6; σ'v = 800 kPa). The compression index (up to two decimal places) of the soil is ______
questions.explanation:
Soil Mechanics | Consolidation

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Void ratio \(e_1 = 1.2\) at effective stress \(\sigma'_{v1} = 50\text{ kPa}\)
    • Void ratio \(e_2 = 0.6\) at effective stress \(\sigma'_{v2} = 800\text{ kPa}\)
  • Aim: Calculate the compression index (\(C_c\)) of the soil (up to two decimal places).

3. Core Concepts:

The compression curve (\(e\) vs. \(\log_{10} \sigma'_v\)) for normally consolidated clay is a straight line.

Compression Index (\(C_c\)): Defined as the slope of the virgin compression line on a semi-logarithmic plot.\[C_c = \dfrac{\Delta e}{\Delta \log_{10} \sigma'_v} = \dfrac{e_1 - e_2}{\log_{10} \left( \dfrac{\sigma'_{v2}}{\sigma'_{v1}} \right)}\]

4. Solution Method:

Directly apply the formula for the compression index using the given points on the straight line.

Sanity Check: \(C_c\) for clayey soils typically ranges between 0.1 and 0.8. The data provided reflects realistic values.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Identify parameters:
    \(e_1 = 1.2\), \(e_2 = 0.6\), \(\sigma'_{v1} = 50\text{ kPa}\), \(\sigma'_{v2} = 800\text{ kPa}\)
  2. Substitute into the formula:\[C_c = \dfrac{1.2 - 0.6}{\log_{10} \left( \dfrac{800}{50} \right)}\]
  3. Evaluate the denominator:\[\dfrac{800}{50} = 16 \implies \log_{10}(16) \approx 1.20412\]
  4. Calculate \(C_c\):\[C_c = \dfrac{0.60}{1.20412} = 0.49829\]
  5. Round off to two decimal places: \(C_c \approx 0.50\)

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.50 | Accepted key range: 0.45 to 0.55

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q44
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: The total horizontal and vertical stresses at a point X in a saturated sandy medium are 170 kPa and 300 kPa, respectively. The static pore-water pressure is 30 kPa. At failure, the excess pore-water pressure is measured to be 94.50 kPa, and the shear stresses on the vertical and horizontal planes passing through the point X are zero. Effective cohesion is 0 kPa and effective angle of internal friction is 36°. The shear strength (in kPa, up to two decimal places) at point X is ______
questions.explanation:
Soil Mechanics | Shear Strength

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Total stresses: \(\sigma_h = 170\text{ kPa}\), \(\sigma_v = 300\text{ kPa}\)
    • Static pore-water pressure: \(u_0 = 30\text{ kPa}\)
    • Excess pore-water pressure at failure: \(\Delta u = 94.50\text{ kPa}\)
    • Shear stress on horizontal and vertical planes = 0 kPa (hence, these are principal planes)
    • Effective shear strength parameters: \(c' = 0\text{ kPa}\), \(\phi' = 36^\circ\)
  • Aim: Determine the shear strength (in kPa) at failure for point X.

3. Core Concepts:

Principal Stresses: Since there are no shear stresses on the vertical and horizontal planes, the applied normal stresses are the principal stresses (\(\sigma_1 = \sigma_v\), \(\sigma_3 = \sigma_h\)).

Effective Stress Principle: \(\sigma' = \sigma - u_{total}\), where total pore pressure at failure \(u_f = u_0 + \Delta u\).

Mohr-Coulomb Failure Criterion: The shear stress at tangency of the Mohr circle with the failure envelope:\[\tau_f = R \cos \phi'\]where radius \(R = \dfrac{\sigma'_1 - \sigma'_3}{2}\).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate the total pore-water pressure at failure.
  2. Determine major (\(\sigma'_1\)) and minor (\(\sigma'_3\)) effective principal stresses.
  3. Compute the radius of the Mohr circle at failure.
  4. Calculate the shear strength on the failure plane using the radius and effective friction angle.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Total Pore Pressure (\(u_f\)):\[u_f = u_0 + \Delta u = 30 + 94.50 = 124.50\text{ kPa}\]
  2. Effective Principal Stresses:\[\sigma'_1 = \sigma_v - u_f = 300 - 124.50 = 175.50\text{ kPa}\]\[\sigma'_3 = \sigma_h - u_f = 170 - 124.50 = 45.50\text{ kPa}\]
  3. Mohr Circle Radius (\(R\)):\[R = \dfrac{\sigma'_1 - \sigma'_3}{2} = \dfrac{175.50 - 45.50}{2} = \dfrac{130.00}{2} = 65.00\text{ kPa}\]
  4. Calculate Shear Strength (\(\tau_f\)):\[\tau_f = R \cos \phi' = 65.00 \times \cos(36^\circ) = 65.00 \times 0.80902 = 52.586\text{ kPa}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 52.59 kPa | Accepted key range: 51.50 to 53.50

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q45
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question:
A group of nine piles in a 3 × 3 square pattern is embedded in a soil strata comprising dense sand underlying recently filled clay layer, as shown in the figure. The perimeter of an individual pile is 126 cm. The size of pile group is 240 cm × 240 cm. The recently filled clay has undrained shear strength of 15 kPa and unit weight of 16 kN/m³.



The negative frictional load (in kN, up to two decimal places) acting on the pile group is ______
questions.explanation:
Foundation Engineering | Deep Foundations (Pile Groups)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Pile group: \(3 \times 3\) (\(n = 9\) piles)
    • Perimeter of one pile: \(p = 126\text{ cm} = 1.26\text{ m}\)
    • Size of pile group: \(B_g \times B_g = 240\text{ cm} \times 240\text{ cm} = 2.4\text{ m} \times 2.4\text{ m}\)
    • Recently filled clay layer thickness: \(L_c = 2\text{ m}\)
    • Clay properties: \(c_u = 15\text{ kPa}\), \(\gamma = 16\text{ kN/m}^3\)
  • Aim: Calculate the total negative frictional load acting on the pile group.

3. Core Concepts:

Negative Skin Friction: Occurs when the surrounding soil (e.g., recently filled soft clay) settles more than the pile, applying a downward drag force.

IS 2911 / Standard Pile Group Guidelines: The design negative skin friction load (\(F_{ng}\)) is the maximum of:

  • Sum of drag forces on individual piles: \(F_{ng,\text{ind}} = n \times (\alpha \cdot c_u \cdot p \cdot L_c)\)
  • Block failure drag force: \(F_{ng,\text{block}} = c_u \cdot P_g \cdot L_c + \gamma \cdot A_g \cdot L_c\)

Standard Assumption: For soft/recently filled clay, the adhesion factor \(\alpha = 1.0\) unless otherwise specified.

4. Solution Method:

Calculate both failure mechanisms (individual vs. block). The pile group experiences the maximum of the two loads because negative skin friction is treated as an applied force, and safety dictates designing for the worst-case drag.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Individual Pile Failure Mechanism (\(F_{ng,\text{ind}}\)):\[F_{ng,ind} = n \times (\alpha \cdot c_u \cdot p \cdot L_c)\]\[F_{ng,ind} = 9 \times (1.0 \times 15\text{ kPa} \times 1.26\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m})\]\[F_{ng,ind} = 9 \times 37.8 = 340.20\text{ kN}\]
  2. Block Failure Mechanism (\(F_{ng,\text{block}}\)):
    • Area of group: \(A_g = 2.4 \times 2.4 = 5.76\text{ m}^2\)
    • Perimeter of group: \(P_g = 4 \times 2.4 = 9.6\text{ m}\)
    \[F_{ng,block} = (c_u \cdot P_g \cdot L_c) + (\gamma \cdot A_g \cdot L_c)\]\[F_{ng,block} = (15 \times 9.6 \times 2) + (16 \times 5.76 \times 2) = 288.00 + 184.32 = 472.32\text{ kN}\]
  3. Determine Final Design Load:\[F_{ng} = \max(340.20\text{ kN},\; 472.32\text{ kN}) = 472.32\text{ kN}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 472.32 kN | Accepted key range: 472.00 to 472.50

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q46
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A three-fluid system (immiscible) is connected to a vacuum pump. The specific gravity values of the fluids (S₁, S₂) are given in the figure.



The gauge pressure value (in kN/m², up to two decimal places) of p₁ is ______
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Manometry & Hydrostatics

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Fluid I: \(S_1 = 0.88\)
    • Fluid II: \(S_2 = 0.95\)
    • Fluid III (Water): \(\gamma_w = 9.81\text{ kN/m}^3\)
    • \(p_{atm} = 95.43\text{ kPa}\)
    • Heights from diagram: Fluid III interface at \(0.5\text{ m}\), Fluid II interface at \(1.0\text{ m}\), Fluid I top surface at \(1.5\text{ m}\)
    • Outer reservoir free surface is at the same level as the \(0.5\text{ m}\) mark
  • Aim: Find the gauge pressure \(p_1\) inside the vacuum tank.

3. Core Concepts:

Hydrostatic Equation: For static fluids, pressure increases going down and decreases going up: \(\Delta p = \pm \gamma h\).

Pascal's Law in Manometry: Pressure in a continuous static fluid is equal at the same horizontal elevation.

Gauge vs Absolute: Gauge pressure equates atmospheric pressure to zero. The value \(95.43\text{ kPa}\) is a distractor meant for absolute pressure calculations.

4. Solution Method:

Since the outer reservoir surface is open to atmosphere and its level aligns with the \(0.5\text{ m}\) interface inside the central tank, the pressure at \(z = 0.5\text{ m}\) is precisely \(p_{atm}\) (or 0 gauge). Write the manometric equation from the vacuum pump (\(p_1\)) downwards to the \(0.5\text{ m}\) elevation.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Identify layer thicknesses inside the tank:
    • Thickness of Fluid I: \(h_1 = 1.5 - 1.0 = 0.5\text{ m}\)
    • Thickness of Fluid II: \(h_2 = 1.0 - 0.5 = 0.5\text{ m}\)
  2. Manometric Equation (start at \(p_1\) gauge and move down to \(z = 0.5\text{ m}\)):\[p_1 + (\gamma_1 \cdot h_1) + (\gamma_2 \cdot h_2) = p_{\text{at } 0.5\text{m}}\]Since \(p_{\text{at } 0.5\text{m, gauge}} = 0\):\[p_1 + (S_1 \cdot \gamma_w \cdot 0.5) + (S_2 \cdot \gamma_w \cdot 0.5) = 0\]
  3. Calculation:\[p_1 + (0.88 \times 9.81 \times 0.5) + (0.95 \times 9.81 \times 0.5) = 0\]\[p_1 + 4.3164 + 4.65975 = 0\]\[p_1 + 8.97615 = 0\]\[p_1 = -8.976\text{ kPa}\](A negative gauge pressure indicates a vacuum, which matches the diagram.)

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: −8.98 kN/m² | Accepted key range: −9.0 to −8.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q47
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: The total rainfall in a catchment of area 1000 km², during a 6 h storm, is 19 cm. The surface runoff due to this storm computed from triangular direct runoff hydrograph is 1×10⁸ m³. The φindex for this storm (in cm/h, up to one decimal place) is ______
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Hydrographs & Infiltration

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Catchment area: \(A = 1000\text{ km}^2 = 10^9\text{ m}^2\)
    • Storm duration: \(t = 6\text{ h}\)
    • Total rainfall: \(P = 19\text{ cm}\)
    • Direct runoff volume: \(V = 1 \times 10^8\text{ m}^3\)
  • Aim: Calculate the \(\phi\)-index for the storm in cm/h.

3. Core Concepts:

Direct Runoff Depth (\(R\)):\[R = \dfrac{\text{Volume of Direct Runoff}}{\text{Catchment Area}}\]

\(\phi\)-index: Represents the average constant infiltration rate over the rainfall duration. Assuming uniform intensity and rainfall rate constantly exceeding infiltration:\[\phi_{\text{index}} = \dfrac{P - R}{t}\]

Note: Mention of "triangular DRH" specifies the hydrograph's shape, but since the raw volume is explicitly provided, shape parameters are irrelevant.

4. Solution Method:

Calculate the direct runoff depth in cm, determine the total infiltration depth, and divide by the time duration.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Runoff Depth (\(R\)):\[R = \dfrac{V}{A} = \dfrac{1 \times 10^8\text{ m}^3}{1 \times 10^9\text{ m}^2} = 0.1\text{ m} = 10\text{ cm}\]
  2. Calculate Total Infiltration:\[\text{Infiltration} = P - R = 19\text{ cm} - 10\text{ cm} = 9\text{ cm}\]
  3. Calculate \(\phi_{\text{index}}\):\[\phi_{\text{index}} = \dfrac{9\text{ cm}}{6\text{ h}} = 1.5\text{ cm/h}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1.5 cm/h | Accepted key range: 1.50 to 1.50

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q48
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A rough pipe of 0.5 m diameter, 300 m length and roughness height of 0.25 mm, carries water (kinematic viscosity = 0.9×10⁻⁶ m²/s) with velocity of 3 m/s. Friction factor (f) for laminar flow is given by f = 64/Rₑ, and for turbulent flow it is given by \( \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{f}} = 2\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{r}{k}\right)+1.74 \), where, Rₑ = Reynolds number, r = radius of pipe, k = roughness height and g = 9.81 m/s². The head loss (in m, up to three decimal places) in the pipe due to friction is ______
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Flow Through Pipes

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Diameter: \(D = 0.5\text{ m}\), Radius: \(r = 0.25\text{ m}\)
    • Length: \(L = 300\text{ m}\)
    • Roughness height: \(k = 0.25\text{ mm} = 0.25 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}\)
    • Kinematic viscosity: \(\nu = 0.9 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^2/\text{s}\), Velocity: \(v = 3\text{ m/s}\)
    • Formula provided: \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{f}} = 2\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{r}{k}\right) + 1.74\)
  • Aim: Compute the head loss (\(h_f\)) in metres due to friction.

3. Core Concepts:

Darcy-Weisbach Equation:\[h_f = \dfrac{f \cdot L \cdot v^2}{2 \cdot g \cdot D}\]where \(f\) is the Darcy friction factor.

Verification of flow regime:\[Re = \dfrac{v \cdot D}{\nu} = \dfrac{3 \times 0.5}{0.9 \times 10^{-6}} = 1.67 \times 10^6 > 4000\quad\text{(Fully turbulent)}\]

The empirical relation provided calculates the Darcy friction factor for rough turbulent pipes directly.

4. Solution Method:

Determine \(r/k\), substitute into the empirical friction factor equation to find \(f\). Then plug \(f\) into the Darcy-Weisbach equation to find \(h_f\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Relative Roughness Ratio (\(r/k\)):\[\dfrac{r}{k} = \dfrac{0.25}{0.25 \times 10^{-3}} = 1000\]
  2. Determine Friction Factor (\(f\)):\[\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{f}} = 2\log_{10}(1000) + 1.74 = 2(3) + 1.74 = 7.74\]\[\sqrt{f} = \dfrac{1}{7.74} = 0.129199\]\[f = (0.129199)^2 \approx 0.016692\]
  3. Compute Head Loss (\(h_f\)):\[h_f = \dfrac{f \cdot L \cdot v^2}{2 \cdot g \cdot D} = \dfrac{0.016692 \times 300 \times (3)^2}{2 \times 9.81 \times 0.5}\]\[h_f = \dfrac{0.016692 \times 2700}{9.81} = \dfrac{45.0684}{9.81} = 4.594\text{ m}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 4.594 m | Accepted key range: 4.50 to 4.70

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q49
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A flocculation tank contains 1800 m³ of water, which is mixed using paddles at an average velocity gradient G of 100/s. The water temperature and the corresponding dynamic viscosity are 30°C and 0.798×10⁻³ Ns/m², respectively. The theoretical power required to achieve the stated value of G (in kW, up to two decimal places) is ______
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Treatment

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Volume of tank: \(V = 1800\text{ m}^3\)
    • Velocity gradient: \(G = 100\text{ s}^{-1}\)
    • Dynamic viscosity at 30°C: \(\mu = 0.798 \times 10^{-3}\text{ Ns/m}^2\)
  • Aim: Calculate the theoretical power (\(P\)) required in kW.

3. Core Concepts:

Camp and Stein's Equation for Flocculation: The temporal mean velocity gradient \(G\) in a mixing tank is given by:\[G = \sqrt{\dfrac{P}{\mu \cdot V}}\]where \(P\) is the power imparted to the water in Watts (W), \(\mu\) is dynamic viscosity, and \(V\) is the tank volume.

4. Solution Method:

Rearrange the velocity gradient equation to solve for \(P\). Obtain the result in Watts, then divide by 1000 to convert to kW.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Rearrange the formula:\[P = G^2 \cdot \mu \cdot V\]
  2. Substitute the values:\[P = (100)^2 \times (0.798 \times 10^{-3}) \times 1800\]\[P = 10000 \times 0.000798 \times 1800 = 7.98 \times 1800 = 14364\text{ W}\]
  3. Convert to kW:\[P = \dfrac{14364}{1000} = 14.364\text{ kW}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 14.36 kW | Accepted key range: 14.00 to 15.00

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q50
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A coal containing 2% sulfur is burned completely to ash in a brick kiln at a rate of 30 kg/min. The sulfur content in the ash was found to be 6% of the initial amount of sulfur present in the coal fed to the brick kiln. The molecular weights of S, H and O are 32, 1 and 16 g/mole, respectively. The annual rate of sulfur dioxide (SO₂) emission from the kiln (in tonnes/year, up to two decimal places) is ______
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Air Pollution

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Coal burn rate = \(30\text{ kg/min}\)
    • Sulfur (S) content in coal = 2%
    • Sulfur retained in ash = 6% of the initial sulfur
    • Molecular weights: S = 32, O = 16 (therefore \(\text{SO}_2 = 32 + 2(16) = 64\))
  • Aim: Calculate the annual rate of sulfur dioxide (\(\text{SO}_2\)) emission in tonnes/year.

3. Core Concepts:

Mass Balance: Total mass of sulfur input = Mass of sulfur in ash + Mass of sulfur emitted into the air.

Stoichiometry of Combustion: \(\text{S} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{SO}_2\)
1 mole of Sulfur (32 kg) produces 1 mole of \(\text{SO}_2\) (64 kg). Therefore, the mass of \(\text{SO}_2\) produced is twice the mass of sulfur combusted.

Unit Conversions: \(1\text{ year} = 365 \times 24 \times 60 = 525600\text{ min}\); \(1\text{ tonne} = 1000\text{ kg}\).

4. Solution Method:

Calculate the mass flow rate of sulfur entering the kiln. Determine the fraction of sulfur that escapes as gas. Convert that mass of sulfur to the corresponding mass of \(\text{SO}_2\). Finally, scale from kg/min to tonnes/year.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Initial Sulfur Feed Rate:\[S_{\text{in}} = 30\text{ kg/min} \times 0.02 = 0.60\text{ kg/min}\]
  2. Sulfur Emitted as Gas:
    Since 6% stays in ash, \(100\% - 6\% = 94\%\) gets emitted.\[S_{\text{emitted}} = 0.60\text{ kg/min} \times 0.94 = 0.564\text{ kg/min}\]
  3. Calculate \(\text{SO}_2\) Emission Rate:
    Using the molar weight ratio \(\left(\dfrac{64}{32} = 2\right)\):\[\text{SO}_{2,\text{emitted}} = 0.564\text{ kg/min} \times 2 = 1.128\text{ kg/min}\]
  4. Convert to Tonnes per Year:\[\text{Annual Rate} = 1.128 \times 60 \times 24 \times 365 = 1.128 \times 525600\text{ kg/year}\]\[= 592876.8\text{ kg/year} = \dfrac{592876.8}{1000} = 592.88\text{ tonnes/year}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 592.88 tonnes/year | Accepted key range: 590.00 to 595.00

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q51
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: At a small water treatment plant which has 4 filters, the rates of filtration and backwashing are 200 m³/d/m² and 1000 m³/d/m², respectively. Backwashing is done for 15 min per day. The maturation, which occurs initially as the filter is put back into service after cleaning, takes 30 min. It is proposed to recover the water being wasted during backwashing and maturation. The percentage increase in the filtered water produced (up to two decimal places) would be ______
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Treatment (Filtration)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Number of filters = 4
    • Rate of filtration (\(R_f\)) = \(200\text{ m}^3/\text{d/m}^2\)
    • Rate of backwashing (\(R_b\)) = \(1000\text{ m}^3/\text{d/m}^2\)
    • Time for backwashing (\(t_b\)) = \(15\text{ min/day}\)
    • Time for maturation (\(t_m\)) = \(30\text{ min/day}\)
  • Aim: Calculate the percentage increase in net filtered water produced if the water wasted during backwashing and maturation is recovered.

3. Core Concepts:

Filtration Cycle: Over a 24-hour day, a filter is not continuously producing water — it has downtimes for backwashing and maturation.

Maturation: Water filtered during the initial 30 minutes after cleaning is of sub-standard quality and is directed to the drain (wasted).

Backwash Water: High-pressure water pumped upwards to clean the filter is taken from the plant's already filtered water (Clear Water Reservoir) and is thus an internal consumption of produced water.

Net Filtered Water: Gross Water Filtered − Water consumed in backwashing.

4. Solution Method:

Since all rates are given per square metre (m²) of filter area, all calculations are performed for a unit area (1 m²) over one day. The number of filters does not change the per-m² ratios.

  1. Determine the exact duration the filter actually produces useful water.
  2. Calculate gross filtered water (\(V_f\)) and water consumed in backwashing (\(V_b\)).
  3. Calculate net filtered water (\(V_{net} = V_f - V_b\)) and water wasted during maturation (\(V_m\)).
  4. Compute the percentage increase if total wasted water (\(V_w = V_b + V_m\)) is recovered.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Time Distribution in a 24-hour Cycle:
    • Backwash downtime = \(15\text{ min} = 0.25\text{ h}\)
    • Maturation downtime = \(30\text{ min} = 0.50\text{ h}\)
    • Effective filtration time: \(t_f = 24 - 0.25 - 0.50 = 23.25\text{ h} = \dfrac{23.25}{24}\text{ days} = 0.96875\text{ days}\)
  2. Volumes per 1 m² per day:
    • Gross useful filtered water:\[V_f = R_f \times t_f = 200 \times 0.96875 = 193.75\text{ m}^3\]
    • Water wasted during maturation:\[V_m = 200 \times \dfrac{30}{1440} = 200 \times 0.020833 = 4.1667\text{ m}^3\]
    • Water utilized for backwashing:\[V_b = 1000 \times \dfrac{15}{1440} = 1000 \times 0.0104167 = 10.4167\text{ m}^3\]
  3. Net and Wasted Water:\[V_{net} = V_f - V_b = 193.75 - 10.4167 = 183.333\text{ m}^3\]\[V_w = V_b + V_m = 10.4167 + 4.1667 = 14.5834\text{ m}^3\]
  4. Percentage Increase:\[\text{\% Increase} = \dfrac{V_w}{V_{net}} \times 100 = \dfrac{14.5834}{183.333} \times 100 = 7.9545\%\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 7.95% | Accepted key range: 7.75 to 7.95

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q52
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
A schematic flow diagram of a completely mixed biological reactor with provision for recycling of solids is shown in the figure.



S₀, S = readily biodegradable soluble BOD, mg/L
Q, Qᵣ, Qw = flow rates, m³/d
X₀, X, Xₑ, X = microorganism concentrations (mixed-liquor volatile suspended solids or MLVSS), mg/L

The mean cell residence time (in days, up to one decimal place) is ______
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Wastewater Engineering (Activated Sludge Process)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Influent flow: \(Q = 15000\text{ m}^3/\text{d}\)
    • Hydraulic detention time: \(t = 2\text{ h}\)
    • MLSS in aeration tank: \(X = 3000\text{ mg/L}\)
    • Waste sludge flow: \(Q_w = 50\text{ m}^3/\text{d}\)
    • Concentration of waste sludge: \(X_u = 10000\text{ mg/L}\)
    • Effluent flow = \(14950\text{ m}^3/\text{d}\), Effluent SS (\(X_e\)) \(\approx 0\text{ mg/L}\)
  • Aim: Determine the mean cell residence time (\(\theta_c\)) in days.

3. Core Concepts:

Mean Cell Residence Time (MCRT or \(\theta_c\)): Also known as Sludge Retention Time (SRT), it is the average time a unit of biomass stays within the biological reactor system.\[\theta_c = \dfrac{\text{Total Mass of Biomass in System}}{\text{Mass of Biomass Leaving System per day}} = \dfrac{V \times X}{(Q_w \times X_u) + (Q - Q_w) \times X_e}\]

Standard Assumption: Biomass in the secondary clarifier is neglected unless its volume is explicitly provided.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate the aeration tank volume (\(V = Q \times t\)).
  2. Compute total mass of microorganisms in the tank (\(M_{in} = V \times X\)).
  3. Compute mass of microorganisms leaving via waste sludge and effluent (\(M_{out}\)).
  4. Divide total mass in tank by mass leaving per day.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Aeration Tank Volume (\(V\)):\[V = Q \times t = 15000\text{ m}^3/\text{d} \times \dfrac{2}{24}\text{ d} = 1250\text{ m}^3\]
  2. Total Mass of Biomass (\(M_{in}\)):\[M_{in} = V \times X = 1250\text{ m}^3 \times 3000\text{ g/m}^3 = 3{,}750{,}000\text{ g} = 3750\text{ kg}\](Using: \(1\text{ mg/L} = 1\text{ g/m}^3\))
  3. Mass of Biomass Leaving (\(M_{out}\)):\[M_{out} = (Q_w \times X_u) + ((Q - Q_w) \times X_e)\]\[M_{out} = (50\text{ m}^3/\text{d} \times 10000\text{ g/m}^3) + (14950\text{ m}^3/\text{d} \times 0) = 500{,}000\text{ g/d} = 500\text{ kg/d}\]
  4. MCRT (\(\theta_c\)):\[\theta_c = \dfrac{M_{in}}{M_{out}} = \dfrac{3750\text{ kg}}{500\text{ kg/d}} = 7.5\text{ days}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 7.5 days | Accepted key range: 7.5 to 7.5

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q53
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: The space mean speed (kmph) and density (vehicles/km) of a traffic stream are linearly related. The free flow speed and jam density are 80 kmph and 100 vehicles/km respectively. The traffic flow (in vehicles/h, up to one decimal place) corresponding to a speed of 40 kmph is ______
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Traffic Engineering

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    • Linear relation between speed and density (Greenshields Model)
    • Free flow speed: \(v_f = 80\text{ kmph}\)
    • Jam density: \(k_j = 100\text{ vehicles/km}\)
    • Operating speed: \(v = 40\text{ kmph}\)
  • Aim: Find the traffic flow (\(q\)) in vehicles/h corresponding to a speed of 40 kmph.

3. Core Concepts:

Greenshields Macroscopic Stream Model: Assumes a linear relationship between space mean speed (\(v\)) and density (\(k\)).\[v = v_f \left(1 - \dfrac{k}{k_j}\right)\]

Fundamental Traffic Equation:\[q = k \times v\]

4. Solution Method:

  1. Substitute given \(v_f\) and \(k_j\) into the Greenshields model.
  2. Use target speed (\(v = 40\text{ kmph}\)) to solve for density (\(k\)).
  3. Multiply calculated \(k\) by \(v\) to find flow (\(q\)).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Determine Density (\(k\)) at \(v = 40\text{ kmph}\):\[40 = 80\left(1 - \dfrac{k}{100}\right)\]\[0.5 = 1 - \dfrac{k}{100} \implies k = 50\text{ vehicles/km}\]
  2. Determine Traffic Flow (\(q\)):\[q = k \times v = 50\text{ veh/km} \times 40\text{ km/h} = 2000\text{ vehicles/h}\]Note: The speed 40 kmph is exactly half of \(v_f = 80\text{ kmph}\), corresponding to the maximum capacity:\[q_{max} = \dfrac{v_f \times k_j}{4} = \dfrac{80 \times 100}{4} = 2000\text{ veh/h}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 2000.0 veh/h | Accepted key range: 2000.0 to 2000.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q54
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question: A 7.5 m wide two-lane road on a plain terrain is to be laid along a horizontal curve of radius 510 m. For a design speed of 100 kmph, super-elevation is provided as per IRC: 73-1980. Consider acceleration due to gravity as 9.81 m/s². The level difference between the inner and outer edges of the road (in m, up to three decimal places) is ______
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Highway Engineering

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Road width: \(W = 7.5\text{ m}\) (Two-lane)
    • Terrain: Plain
    • Horizontal curve radius: \(R = 510\text{ m}\)
    • Design speed: \(V = 100\text{ kmph}\)
    • \(g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2\)
    • Design Code: IRC 73-1980
  • Aim: Calculate the level difference between the inner and outer edges of the fully super-elevated road.

3. Core Concepts:

Super-elevation Design as per IRC:

  1. Calculate theoretical super-elevation (\(e_{calc}\)) for 75% of design speed, completely neglecting lateral friction:\[e_{calc} = \dfrac{(0.75 \times v)^2}{g \times R}\]
  2. Check against maximum allowable limit. For plain and rolling terrain: \(e_{max} = 0.07\) (7%).
  3. If \(e_{calc} > 0.07\), limit provision to \(0.07\) and check if required lateral friction \(f \le 0.15\).

Level Difference (\(E\)): \(E = e_{provided} \times W\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Convert design speed from kmph to m/s.
  2. Compute \(e_{calc}\) using the fundamental formula.
  3. Compare \(e_{calc}\) with IRC limit (0.07) to find the provided \(e\).
  4. Check lateral friction (\(f\)) at full design speed to ensure safety.
  5. Multiply the provided \(e\) by the pavement width to get the level difference.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Velocity Conversion:\[v = 100 \times \dfrac{5}{18} = 27.778\text{ m/s}\]
  2. Theoretical Super-elevation (\(e_{calc}\)):\[e_{calc} = \dfrac{(0.75 \times 27.778)^2}{9.81 \times 510} = \dfrac{(20.8335)^2}{5003.1} = \dfrac{434.03}{5003.1} = 0.08675\]Since \(e_{calc}\,(0.08675) > e_{max}\,(0.07)\) for plain terrain, restrict to \(e_{provided} = 0.07\).
  3. Check Lateral Friction (\(f\)):\[e_{provided} + f_{req} = \dfrac{v^2}{gR} = \dfrac{(27.778)^2}{9.81 \times 510} = \dfrac{771.61}{5003.1} = 0.1542\]\[f_{req} = 0.1542 - 0.07 = 0.0842\]Since \(f_{req}\,(0.0842) < f_{max}\,(0.15)\), providing \(e = 0.07\) is safe and no speed restriction is needed.
  4. Level Difference (\(E\)):\[E = e_{provided} \times W = 0.07 \times 7.5\text{ m} = 0.525\text{ m}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.525 m | Accepted key range: 0.520 to 0.530

questions.title: GATE CE 2018 Set 2 | CE Q55
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question: An aerial photograph of a terrain having an average elevation of 1400 m is taken at a scale of 1:7500. The focal length of the camera is 15 cm. The altitude of the flight above mean sea level (in m, up to one decimal place) is ______
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Photogrammetry

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Average elevation of terrain: \(h = 1400\text{ m}\)
    • Scale of photograph: \(S = 1:7500\)
    • Focal length of camera: \(f = 15\text{ cm} = 0.15\text{ m}\)
  • Aim: Find the altitude of the flight above Mean Sea Level (\(H\)) in metres.

3. Core Concepts:

Scale of a Vertical Photograph: The scale over a horizontal terrain of given elevation correlates the focal length of the camera with the flying height above that terrain level.\[S = \dfrac{f}{H - h}\]where \(S\) = scale of photograph, \(f\) = focal length, \(H\) = flying height above MSL, \(h\) = average terrain elevation above MSL.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Ensure unit consistency — both \(f\) and elevations (\(H, h\)) must be in metres.
  2. Substitute given values into the scale equation.
  3. Solve algebraically for \(H\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Unit Conversion and Setup:\[f = 15\text{ cm} = 0.15\text{ m}, \quad S = \dfrac{1}{7500}\]
  2. Evaluate the Scale Equation:\[\dfrac{1}{7500} = \dfrac{0.15}{H - 1400}\]\[H - 1400 = 7500 \times 0.15 = 1125\]
  3. Solve for \(H\):\[H = 1400 + 1125 = 2525\text{ m}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 2525.0 m | Accepted key range: 2520.0 to 2530.0
